title: Squeezing Data: Compression
objective: After this level you can explain why photos and video can shrink to a fraction of their size, and what lossy compression throws away.
summary: Lossless compression removes repetition and restores data exactly; lossy compression like JPEG discards detail the eye misses; video stores only what changes between frames.

cards.headline: Level 3's photo: about 73 MB of pixels, about 3.6 MB as a JPEG.
cards.body: The saved file is about a twentieth of the raw pixels, and it still looks sharp. Where did the rest go? Some of it was repetition, and some of it was detail your eyes were never going to miss.

cards.headline: Lossless: say it shorter
cards.body: Lossless compression can be reversed to give back the original data exactly. It works by cutting repetition. The simplest trick, run-length encoding, replaces a run of repeated items with a count and one copy: instead of the same white pixel over and over, store how many, then one white pixel. Zip files are lossless, which matters for text, where every character has to come back exactly.

cards.headline: Lossy: drop what you won't see
cards.body: Lossy compression goes further and loses some detail for good. JPEG averages out small variations in color and throws away what the human eye cannot see, which is how Level 3's photo shrank about 20 to 1 with practically invisible loss. That works for pictures and voices, where small errors spread over scattered spots are hard to notice. On your bank statement, it would be a disaster.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: lossless gives back every bit exactly. Lossy gives back something that only looks or sounds the same.

cards.fact: Video shrinks by storing only what changes between frames.
cards.context: Instead of saving every frame whole, standards such as MPEG store the slight differences between one frame and the next. Where little moves, like a face talking against a still wall, little needs storing.

cards.headline: Data: squeezed
learned: Run-length encoding: a count and one copy
Lossy JPEG discards what the eye can't see
Video stores only the changes between frames

questions.prompt: How does video compression avoid saving every frame whole?

options.label: It saves only every tenth frame and skips the rest
options.rationale: Frames aren't skipped; changes are stored.

options.label: It stores only the differences between successive frames
It turns the video into black and white
options.rationale: Color is kept; repetition between frames is cut.

questions.explanation: Standards such as MPEG store only the slight differences between one frame and the next.

questions.prompt: Why is lossy compression fine for a photo but not for a text document?

options.label: Text files are always too small to compress
Photos contain no repeated patterns worth removing
Picture errors are hard to spot; text must come back exact
Lossy compression can only be used on colored files
options.rationale: The issue is exactness, not color.

questions.explanation: Lossy compression suits images and voice, where scattered small errors go unnoticed; text needs every character back exactly, so it's compressed losslessly.

questions.prompt: Level 3's 73 MB photo became about 3.6 MB as a JPEG. Where did most of the saving come from?

options.label: The camera took fewer pixels
options.rationale: The pixel count stayed the same.

options.label: Each pixel was shrunk to half its size
options.rationale: The pixels stayed the same; detail was discarded.

options.label: The JPEG file was stored in the cloud
options.rationale: Where it's stored doesn't change its size.

options.label: Discarding color detail the eye can't see

questions.explanation: JPEG is lossy: it averages color variation and discards what the eye can't see, easily reaching about 20 to 1.
